price_per_million.source: copied from reasoning_models_v1 (confirmed 2026-11-11); thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: play-type labeling from play-by-play and derived possession records
label error and outcome-derived labels (foul endings, assisted flag)
sequencing of events across and within possessions
regression to the mean and selection in play-type PPP comparisons
methodological_questions: Can a DRIVE and a subsequent PNR be identified reliably enough in the derived records to define exposure?
Is the PNR label independent of the PPP outcome, or is it built from proxies that are calibrated or outcome-linked?
How should the effect be estimated while controlling for player, lineup, opponent, game state and shot clock?
Is there enough drive-then-PNR exposure for power, and how should multiplicity across drive definitions be handled?
Can a preceding drive be defined without look-ahead or leakage from the same possession?

historical_evidence.finding: OTHER PPP is inflated by 36% foul endings. DRIVE sits 12pp below the foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK). PNR shows a 22% foul rate. Only 0.7% of 50,668 possessions map to a real play type via initiation_type. Verdict: artifact_found.

The assisted flag exists only on makes, which produced SPOT_UP 2.83 PPP (100% makes). After the classifier was rewritten, SPOT_UP was about 1.16. The record calls it an engineering discovery that poisoned simulation.

The label audit failed overall: OTHER was 20.2% vs a <10% target, 40.8% of labels were low confidence, and DRIVE foul-draw was 1.7% vs a 14-22% benchmark. Most play types had PPP above the benchmark band. Limits recorded: label error, leakage, small sample. Verdict: tool_eval_fail.

The backfill verification failed. PNR was 28.7% (band 20-28%), and 3100 games had team PNR above 33%. 82.8% of PNR labels were proxy_calibrated, team identity checks failed, and PULL_UP was 0-2% for many 2024-25 teams. PNR PPP of 0.948 passed. n=921,514 possessions.

2024-25 shot-level PNR share of half-court shots ranged from 7.6% (OKC) to 13.8% (IND). The rates were a calibration input for PBPProxyPNR, and later logs show calibrated PNR at about 17.9-19.6% of possessions.
On-ball coverage labels were confident for only 14.9% (DET) and 3.3% (ORL) of possessions. switches_on was unpopulated. Failure type: A_unanswerable, limited by label error and small sample.
The PNR possession share jump of +12.1pp between regular season and playoffs may reflect tagging differences. Risks recorded: label error and mechanical floor.

DRIVE PPP was 1.198 in the regular season vs 0.912 in the playoffs, and PNR PPP was -0.173 lower in the playoffs. The analysis was team-level with no CIs. It says nothing about drive-then-PNR sequencing.
Across playoff game buckets, DRIVE PPP went from 0.889 to 0.949 and PNR changed by +0.087. The record notes selection and regression-to-the-mean caveats, with no CIs.
A preceding-possession effect on next-possession PPP was examined. Cells had n_after of 32-95 with no multiplicity correction, and the record flags drift/nonstationarity.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating play-type PPP differences as real efficiency without checking labels
failed_approaches.why: Foul-ending leakage inflated OTHER and distorted DRIVE and PNR. The record states a labelling or construction artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Possession-level play types inferred from play-by-play with an outcome-linked flag
failed_approaches.why: The assisted flag exists only on makes, which produced an artifactual PPP.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Backfilled play-type labels used as if they matched league distributions and team identities
failed_approaches.why: The verification failed, PNR labels were mostly proxy-calibrated, and the failure mechanism is recorded as an artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferred play-type labels used for adaptation findings
failed_approaches.why: The audit recorded systematic label issues, including a DRIVE foul-draw rate far below benchmark, and said they undermine adaptation findings.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Labeling on-ball context from matchup and play-by-play fields
failed_approaches.why: Confident label rates were low and the fields were unpopulated, so the question was recorded as untestable.

evidence_establishes: No retrieved record tests whether a teammate drive before a PNR changes PNR PPP.

The derived play-type records have documented label problems: foul-ending leakage, an outcome-linked assisted flag, and proxy-calibrated PNR labels (82.8%). These bear directly on both DRIVE and PNR PPP.
DRIVE and PNR PPP differ systematically between regular season and playoffs at team level (FAM:SF-APPS-011). This is a context-dependence signal, not a test of the sequence.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a preceding drive raises, lowers or leaves unchanged PNR PPP.
Whether drive-then-PNR sequences occur often enough in the data to give power.
Whether the current labels have been repaired since the cited audits. The records do not say.
Any effect size or CI for sequential or lagged play-type effects, since none were recorded with CIs.
own_inferences: 'Any teammate DRIVE' is a universal claim. It should be recast as a pooled average effect plus heterogeneity by drive type, otherwise it cannot be falsified cleanly.

If PNR labels were proxy-calibrated from shot or outcome features, the PNR label may depend on the possession result, which would bias PPP. A drive before a PNR may also be a side effect of how the labeler segments possessions.
Non-shot drives are likely invisible in play-by-play, so exposure may be mismeasured and attenuated toward zero.
Drive-then-PNR sequences are probably not randomly assigned. Better offenses, certain lineups, and drive-and-kick ball movement (which also shortens the shot clock) would confound a naive PPP gap.

A cross-possession drive (a prior possession) and a within-possession drive (earlier action in the same possession) are different estimands. The within-possession version risks look-ahead and label-construction leakage.
Foul-ending share differs between PNR and DRIVE labels, so a PPP comparison could be driven by free throws rather than shot quality.
The 2025-26 playoffs finish after the question date (2026-06-14). Any held-out confirmation must be frozen in advance.
uncertainties: Whether the current derived graph database fixes the problems found in the earlier audits.
The true count of drive-then-PNR sequences, and whether the label provenance can separate exact from proxy PNRs.
Whether tracking-quality fields can identify non-shot drives. The data catalog was not checked.
The size of the true effect, if any.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the history, a straightforward PPP regression would look feasible. The records show the PNR and DRIVE labels are artifact-prone (foul leakage, outcome-linked flags, proxy calibration), so I changed the decision to proceed_with_changes. A label-validity gate must pass first, and the result must be treated as artifact-prone until it does. The estimand must also be narrowed.

blocking_constraints.text: 82.8% of PNR labels were proxy-calibrated and the DRIVE foul rate is far below benchmark (FAM:SF-APPA-030, FAM:SF-CHT-025, FAM:SF-APPM-014). Exposure and outcome may both be mislabeled.
Earlier labelers used outcome-linked features (assisted flag, foul endings) that can make PPP depend on the label (FAM:SF-PAP-096).
Drive-then-PNR sequences with exact PNR labels may be too few, and non-shot drives may be unobservable.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record tests drive-before-PNR sequencing. The related records establish that play-type labels are artifact-prone and that regular-season and playoff PPP differ at team level.

risks.text: Proxy-calibrated PNR labels and sparse DRIVE labels can misclassify exposure and outcome.
Labels built from makes, assists or fouls make PPP depend on the labeler.
A drive that occurs within the same possession, or after a PNR is defined, can be selected on later events. Exposure must be fixed using only information before the PNR's screen time.
Player quality, lineup, opponent, defensive scheme, score, shot clock, and drive-and-kick ball movement all affect PPP and the chance of a drive.
Qualifying sequences may be few, especially when restricted to exact labels.
Past work with cells of 30-95 possessions and no CIs shows that thin cells give unstable estimates.
Many drive definitions (distance, outcome, driver role, recency) and season and playoff splits invite forking paths.
Labeler versions, league tendencies and playoff vs regular-season context change across 2022-26.
If drives are triggered by prior good or bad possessions, or selected on team strength, regression to the mean can produce spurious effects.
Foul and free-throw endings and possession-ending rules can fix a PPP floor or ceiling differently across labels.

design.estimand: Average within-team difference in PNR points per possession (PPP) when a same-team DRIVE occurred in the 8 seconds of game time immediately before the PNR initiation, vs matched PNRs without a drive. Teammate drive means a drive by a player other than the PNR ball handler. Drive-before-PNR is measured pre-initiation only. Heterogeneity by drive type and drive outcome is secondary and exploratory.
design.unit: PNR possession (exact labels only), clustered by team-game and nested by offense and defense.
design.sample: Regular seasons 2022-23 to 2024-25 for development and estimation. 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13) as a frozen out-of-time confirmation. 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21) as a separate descriptive check, not pooled with the regular season. Restrict to half-court PNRs with labels that are not proxy-calibrated and not outcome-derived. Exclude possessions starting off turnovers or fouls, and garbage time.
design.power: First count exposed and unexposed exact-label PNRs. Power is checked before looking at PPP: report the minimum detectable PPP difference at 80% power using the observed PNR PPP SD (about 1.1-1.2 in an assumed typical range, to be measured) and the cluster-adjusted effective n. If the minimum detectable effect exceeds 0.08 PPP, the result is reported as untestable at useful power and not interpreted.
design.controls: Offensive and defensive team, lineup or ball-handler and screener fixed effects, opponent quality, score margin, period, shot-clock time at PNR start, home and away, season, rest. Matching or doubly robust estimation (propensity of a prior drive from pre-treatment covariates). Drive and PNR labels must come from versions with auditable provenance (exact vs proxy). Foul-ending possessions are modelled separately: report PPP with and without free throws, and effective FG% on non-foul endings.
design.falsification: (1) Label-validity gate: before any outcome analysis, audit a hand-checked sample of PNR and DRIVE labels and require the PNR label to be unrelated to make, assist and foul outcomes conditional on shot type; if not, stop. (2) Placebo exposure: a drive 8-16 seconds after the PNR, or a drive by the opposing team, should show no effect. (3) Negative control outcome: the previous possession's PPP should not be affected. (4) Permutation of drive timing within team-game. (5) Re-estimate with proxy-calibrated PNR labels and check whether the result is label-dependent.
design.multiplicity: One pre-registered primary test: the pooled effect on PNR PPP. Secondary analyses (drive type, distance, outcome, playoffs) are labelled exploratory and corrected using Holm or false-discovery-rate control across the stated family. No extra drive definitions are added after seeing outcomes.
design.decision_rule: Supported if the primary effect is positive with the 95% cluster-robust CI excluding zero in development, the confirmation season has the same sign with CI excluding zero, the placebo and negative-control tests are null, and the result is robust to excluding proxy labels and foul endings. Rejected if the CI lies entirely within a +/-0.03 PPP equivalence band with adequate power. Artifact if the label gate fails or placebo effects are comparable to the primary effect. Otherwise inconclusive.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game play-by-play and derived play-type possession records as of 2026-06-14 for seasons 2022-23 to 2025-26. The labeler and graph database version and commit, and a label-provenance field distinguishing exact from proxy PNR, are recorded before analysis. The 2025-26 playoffs are partial before 2026-06-21 and are frozen only when complete.

methodological_questions: Can a drive be reliably identified from play-by-play data and linked to a subsequent PNR possession?
How should the effect of a preceding drive on PNR PPP be estimated while controlling for confounders such as player quality, lineup, opponent, and shot clock?
Does the derived play-type labeling introduce label error or outcome-derived labels that bias PPP comparisons?
Is there enough exposure (sequences of drive then PNR) for adequate statistical power, and how to handle multiple testing across definitions?
Are there look-ahead or leakage risks in defining a preceding drive using information from the same possession?
args.query: Does a teammate drive immediately before a pick-and-roll raise PNR points per possession; play-type labeling and data quality in play-by-play derived possession records

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 10 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-14, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether to call more tools or just wrap up, and leaning toward finishing now. The question's claim that any teammate DRIVE before a PNR raises PNR PPP is a broad "any" claim and fairly vague. Several caveats stand out: the PNR labels are mostly proxy-calibrated at 82.8%, there's DRIVE foul leakage, the PNR foul rate is 22%, and an assisted-flag leak is present.

I'm considering whether the preceding drive actually shows up in the play-by-play, since drives without shots can't be observed. Possession sequencing, offensive rebounds, and kick-outs could all confound a drive-then-PNR link. The data is also partial for 2025-26, with playoffs not complete until after the question date, so I'd pre-register on regular-season data and mention the data version.
